q: What does scalability mean, and how do I tell if a system has it?

Scalability is the ability to handle more load (users, requests, data) by adding resources, without the cost or latency growing out of control. You check it by asking: if load grows 10x, what breaks first, and can we fix it by adding machines? A system scales well when capacity grows roughly in line with the resources you add, and badly when one shared part (often the database) caps everything.
load, bottleneck, capacity
A site handles 100 requests per second on one server. Adding a second server should give about 200. If the single database caps at 150, the database, not the web tier, is the real limit.
A shop that serves ten customers happily should still work with ten thousand, without a rebuild.

What is the difference between availability and reliability?

Availability is the share of time a system is up and answering. Reliability is how correctly it behaves over time: producing right results without failing or losing data. A system can be available but unreliable (it answers quickly with wrong or stale data) or reliable but unavailable (correct, but down for maintenance). Interviews often want you to separate the two and say which one a feature needs.
uptime, correctness, nines
A payment page that always loads but sometimes records the wrong amount is available but not reliable. A bank that goes down for a nightly batch is reliable but not always available.
Availability: is the shop open when I arrive? Reliability: does it give me the right thing when it is open?

What do 'the nines' of availability mean in real downtime?

Availability is quoted as a percentage over time. Approximate downtime per year: 99% is about 3.65 days, 99.9% about 8.8 hours, 99.99% about 53 minutes, and 99.999% about 5 minutes. Chained dependencies multiply: two components at 99.9% each give roughly 99.8% together, because either failing hurts. This is why designs add redundancy and avoid long serial chains.
SLA, redundancy, serial dependencies
If your checkout depends on five services each at 99.9%, the whole path is about 99.5%, roughly 44 hours of possible trouble a year.
Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by ten times, and each one costs far more to reach.
What happens when a design has a single point of failure (SPOF)?

A single point of failure is any part whose failure takes the whole system down: one server, one database, one load balancer, one network link, even one person who holds knowledge. When it fails, everything depending on it stops, and the blast radius is the whole product. You remove SPOFs by adding redundancy (a standby or a second active copy), automatic failover and health checks, then testing the failover for real.
redundancy, failover, blast radius
A site has ten web servers but one load balancer. The servers are fine, yet the LB crashes at 9 p.m. and the site is unreachable until someone restarts it. A redundant LB pair would have kept it up.
One lock on the only door: if it jams, nobody gets in.

How do I spot single points of failure in a design diagram?

Trace a request from the user to the data and back. At each box, ask whether there is a second copy, whether failover is automatic, and what the box depends on. Also check hidden ones: DNS, certificates, a shared config store, a single cloud region or zone, one queue, one deployment pipeline, one on-call person. Each yes-it-is-alone answer is a candidate SPOF to fix or to accept knowingly.
architecture review, redundancy
Diagram: client, CDN, one API gateway, three services, one primary database. The gateway and the primary are SPOFs; the three services are not.
Walk the path of one request and ask of every box: if this dies, what still works?
What is the difference between latency, throughput and bandwidth?

Latency is the time for one request to complete (milliseconds). Throughput is how many requests or units of work finish per second. Bandwidth is the maximum data a link can carry per second. They interact: a wide road does not make one car faster, and high throughput can come with higher latency when queues build. Interviews expect you to say which one a design is optimising.
p99, percentile, tail latency
A video call needs low latency; a nightly file copy needs high throughput; a 4K stream needs bandwidth. A request taking 200 ms, with 50 handled at once, gives roughly 250 requests per second.
Latency is how long one car takes. Throughput is how many cars finish per hour. Bandwidth is how wide the road is.

Why does 'key mod number of servers' break when servers change?

If you place data on server number (hash of key mod N), adding or removing one server changes N, so most keys map to different servers. For a cache, that means nearly everything misses at once and the database is flooded; for a data store, it means massive data movement. Consistent hashing fixes this so only a small fraction of keys move.
hash, rebalancing, cache miss storm
With 4 servers and 1,000,000 keys, going to 5 servers by mod-N moves about 80% of keys. With consistent hashing it moves roughly 1/5, about 20%.
Imagine assigning students to classrooms by roll number; add a classroom and almost everyone has to move.
What is consistent hashing, and how does the ring work?

Hash both servers and keys onto the same circular space (the ring). A key is stored on the first server found going clockwise from its position. When a server is added, it takes over only the keys between it and the previous server; when one is removed, only its keys move to the next server. Virtual nodes (each server placed at many points) spread load evenly and make rebalancing smoother.
ring, virtual nodes, rebalancing
Servers A, B, C on the ring. Key 'user:42' hashes between A and B, so it goes to B. Add D between A and B: only keys between A and D move to D; everything else stays.
Picture a clock face: servers sit at positions on it, and each key belongs to the next server clockwise.

How do you handle a hot key (one very popular item)?
What go wrong with consistent hashing, and how do virtual nodes help?

With few servers placed randomly, slices of the ring are uneven, so some servers carry far more keys. When a server dies, all its load falls on one neighbour, which may then fail too. Virtual nodes give each physical server many positions, so slices are small and mixed and a failure spreads across many servers. Weights can give bigger machines more virtual nodes. Hot keys are still a separate problem that hashing does not solve.
load skew, failure spread
A cluster of 3 servers with one virtual node each ends up 60/30/10. With 100 virtual nodes each, the split is close to 33/33/33.
If one server gets a huge slice of the clock face, it gets most of the work.
What is the CAP theorem, and what does a network partition really mean?

CAP says that during a network partition, a distributed system cannot be both fully consistent (every read sees the latest write) and fully available (every request gets an answer). Partitions are a fact of life, so the real choice is between consistency and availability when one happens. When there is no partition you can usually have both, and trade latency against consistency instead (the idea behind the PACELC extension).
CP, AP, partition tolerance, PACELC
During a split, a balance service may reject writes (consistent, less available) while a 'likes' counter keeps accepting them and fixes the counts later (available, eventually consistent).
If the phone line between two bank branches is cut, each branch must choose: refuse customers, or serve them with possibly stale balances.

What is the CAP theorem in plain words?
How do I choose between CP and AP for a feature?

Decide per feature. Choose consistency when wrong data causes real harm: money, inventory for the last item, seat booking, permissions. Choose availability when staleness is harmless and downtime is costly: feeds, view counts, recommendations, product catalogue pages. State the compromise out loud: for example 'refuse the write and show a retry message' versus 'accept it and reconcile later'.
trade-off, reconciliation
Seat booking: CP, show 'try again' rather than sell the same seat twice. Home-page recommendations: AP, serve yesterday's list if the service is cut off.
Ask what is worse: showing nothing for a while, or showing something slightly wrong.
What is the OSI model, and does a system designer really need it?

The OSI model describes networking in seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. In practice you mostly need four ideas: the network layer (IP addresses and routing), the transport layer (TCP or UDP and ports), and the application layer (HTTP, DNS and similar protocols), plus the link underneath. Knowing the layers helps you say where a problem sits, for example 'this is a TCP connection issue, not an HTTP bug'.
layers, TCP/IP model
A page fails to load. Layer thinking: can I reach the IP (network)? does the port accept connections (transport)? does the server return a correct HTTP response (application)?
A layered postal system: envelope, sorting centre, truck, road. Each layer does one job and trusts the one below.
What is an IP address, and what are IPv4, IPv6, public and private addresses?

An IP address identifies a device on a network. IPv4 uses 32 bits (about 4.3 billion addresses, now scarce); IPv6 uses 128 bits and effectively removes the shortage. Private ranges (such as 10.x.x.x or 192.168.x.x) are for use inside a network and are not routable on the internet; devices share one public address through NAT. Servers that must be reachable have public addresses, usually behind a load balancer.
IPv4, IPv6, NAT, subnet
Your phone at home has a private address like 192.168.1.20; the router presents one public address to websites.
A house address: the street number is the network, the door number is the device.
What is the difference between TCP and UDP, and when would I pick each?

TCP sets up a connection, numbers the data, retransmits what is lost and delivers it in order, so it is reliable but adds delay. UDP just sends packets with no guarantee of delivery or order, so it is fast and light. Use TCP when correctness matters (web pages, APIs, file transfer, databases). Use UDP when speed matters more than perfection or when the app adds its own handling (live video or voice, games, DNS lookups, and QUIC, which HTTP/3 runs on).
reliability, handshake, QUIC
A bank transfer over TCP: every byte must arrive. A video call over UDP: a dropped frame is skipped rather than waiting for a resend.
TCP is registered post with tracking and re-delivery; UDP is dropping postcards in the box and hoping.
What happens inside a TCP connection: the handshake and why it costs time?

TCP opens with a three-step handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), costing one round trip before data flows. HTTPS adds a TLS handshake on top. This is why new connections are expensive and why servers reuse them (keep-alive, connection pools). Far-away users pay more because each round trip is long. Under loss or congestion, TCP slows down, which can raise latency suddenly.
SYN, round trip, keep-alive
A user 150 ms away pays about 150 ms for the TCP handshake, plus more for TLS, before the first byte of the page request even starts.
Before talking you say 'Hello, can you hear me?', 'Yes, can you?', 'Yes.' Only then do you start the real conversation.
What is HTTP, and what changed across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3?

HTTP is the request-response protocol of the web. HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection (browsers open several). HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection and compresses headers. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (on UDP), reducing delays from lost packets and connection setup. In design discussions, mention methods (GET, POST), status codes, headers, caching and keep-alive rather than protocol internals.
multiplexing, headers, QUIC
A page with 80 small files: HTTP/1.1 queues them across several connections; HTTP/2 sends them over one connection together.
The same conversation, with progressively better ways to carry many requests at once.

What are HTTPS and TLS, and what do they protect?

HTTPS is HTTP carried inside TLS. TLS provides encryption (nobody on the path can read it), integrity (changes are detected) and authentication (a certificate issued by a trusted authority proves the server's identity). The client checks the certificate, both sides agree on keys, and traffic is then encrypted. It does not protect against a malicious or hacked server itself, and expired certificates break connections.
certificate, handshake, encryption
A public Wi-Fi snooper sees only scrambled bytes for an HTTPS login, but could read an HTTP one.
A sealed, tamper-evident envelope with the sender's identity checked, instead of a postcard.
What is DNS, and how does a lookup actually work?

DNS maps names (shop.example.com) to IP addresses. Your device asks a recursive resolver (usually your ISP or a public one), which checks its cache, otherwise asks the root servers, then the top-level domain servers, then the domain's authoritative server, and returns the answer. Results are cached for a time set by the TTL. Record types include A/AAAA (addresses), CNAME (alias), MX (mail) and TXT.
resolver, TTL, A record, CNAME
A migration plan sets TTL to 60 seconds a day before moving servers, so clients pick up the new IP within a minute.
The internet's phone book: you know the name, DNS tells you the number.

What happens when DNS fails or returns a stale answer?

If DNS fails, users cannot resolve your name and the site looks down, even if servers are healthy. A long TTL means a changed IP takes time to spread (stale answers), and a very short TTL raises load and dependence on the resolvers. Mitigations: several name-server providers, sensible TTLs, health-checked failover records, and monitoring from outside your network. Many big outages have been DNS-related.
outage, TTL, failover
A company moves to a new data centre but DNS still points to the old IP for hours because of a 24-hour TTL.
If the phone book is wrong or missing, people cannot find your shop even though it is open.
What is the difference between a proxy and a reverse proxy?

A forward proxy sits in front of clients and makes requests for them (privacy, filtering, caching in a company network). A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and receives requests for them: it can terminate TLS, balance load, cache, compress, rate limit and hide internal servers. Nginx, HAProxy and cloud gateways are common reverse proxies. A load balancer is a kind of reverse proxy.
nginx, TLS termination, gateway
Users hit shop.example.com; a reverse proxy sends /images to a static server and /api to the application servers.
A forward proxy shops on your behalf; a reverse proxy is the receptionist who decides which back-office handles your request.
What is a checksum, and why do systems use checksums?

A checksum is a small value calculated from data (CRC32, MD5, SHA-256 and others). The receiver recomputes it and compares to detect corruption in transit or storage. Simple checksums catch accidental errors; cryptographic hashes also resist deliberate tampering. Used in TCP segments, file downloads, storage systems, replication and backup verification. A checksum detects problems; it does not repair them (error-correcting codes or replicas do).
hash, integrity, CRC
A downloaded installer shows a SHA-256 value; if your computed value differs, the file is corrupted or altered.
A short fingerprint of the data: if one letter changes, the fingerprint changes.
What does a load balancer do, and where does it sit?

A load balancer distributes incoming requests across several servers so no one is overloaded, removes unhealthy servers using health checks, and gives users a single address. It can sit in front of web servers, between services, or in front of databases. It enables horizontal scaling and rolling updates, and is itself a component you must make redundant.
health check, redundancy
Three app servers sit behind an LB. When one fails its health check, the LB stops sending it traffic and users do not notice.
The host at a restaurant who sends each new group to a free table.

What is a load balancer and what happens if it fails?
What is the difference between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing?

A Layer 4 balancer works on IP addresses and ports (TCP or UDP) and forwards connections without reading content: very fast and simple. A Layer 7 balancer understands HTTP, so it can route by path, host, header or cookie, terminate TLS, rewrite requests and apply rules per URL. L7 is more flexible and costs more per request. Many systems use L4 at the edge and L7 inside.
TCP, HTTP routing, TLS termination
L7 sends /api/* to the API pool and /static/* to a cache pool. L4 just spreads TCP connections across the same pool.
L4 reads only the address on the envelope; L7 opens the letter to decide who handles it.
Which load balancing algorithms exist, and how do I choose?

Round robin rotates through servers. Weighted round robin favours bigger machines. Least connections picks the server with the fewest active connections. Least response time picks the fastest. IP or key hashing keeps the same client on the same server (and consistent hashing limits disruption when servers change). Choose round robin for similar, short requests; least connections for long or uneven requests; hashing when you need stickiness or cache locality.
round robin, least connections, hashing
Video transcoding jobs vary from 5 seconds to 5 minutes: least connections works better than round robin, which could pile long jobs on one server.
Different ways to hand out tables: take turns, give it to the emptiest, or always seat regulars at the same table.
What are sticky sessions, and what goes wrong with them?

Sticky sessions send a user to the same server each time, usually because session state lives in that server's memory. Problems: uneven load, lost sessions when the server dies or is replaced, and harder deployments. The better design makes servers stateless and keeps session data in a shared store (Redis or a database) or in a signed token, so any server can handle any request.
stateless, session store
A user logs in on server A. A deploy restarts A, and the user is logged out. With sessions in Redis, any server would have continued.
Always seating a regular at the same table is nice until that table's waiter is overwhelmed or goes home.
How does DNS load balancing work, and what are its limits?

The authoritative DNS server returns different IP addresses (round robin, weighted or based on the client's location) so clients are spread across servers or regions. It is simple and works globally. Limits: caching means changes and failures take time to take effect (TTL), clients may keep using a dead address, and DNS does not know real server load. It is often used to route to regional load balancers, not to individual servers.
geo-DNS, TTL, failover
A global product gives European users the Frankfurt address and US users the Virginia address using geo-DNS.
The phone book lists several numbers for your shop and hands out a different one each time.
What is anycast routing, and how does it differ from unicast?

With anycast, the same IP address is announced from many locations, and network routing delivers each packet to the nearest or best-reachable one. It reduces latency, absorbs DDoS attacks across sites and gives automatic failover when a site stops announcing. Used by CDNs and public DNS. Limits: routes can shift mid-connection, so stateful long connections need care, and you do not fully control which site a user reaches.
BGP, CDN, DDoS
A public DNS service uses one anycast address; a user in Mumbai reaches a Mumbai node, a user in Paris reaches a Paris node.
Many shops share one phone number; the call connects to the nearest.
What happens when a load balancer misroutes or its health check is wrong?

A health check that is too shallow (only 'port is open') keeps sending traffic to a server that is up but broken. One that is too strict can remove all servers at once during a brief slowdown, causing a self-inflicted outage. Fixes: check a meaningful endpoint, require several failures before removal, add slow-start for new servers, cap removals, and alert when many servers go unhealthy together.
health checks, cascading failure, slow start
A database blip makes every server's health check fail; the LB drops all of them and returns errors even though the servers recover in seconds.
The host who thinks an empty table is full, or sends guests to a closed one.

q: What is an API, and what makes one well designed?

An API is a defined contract for how one piece of software asks another to do something. A good API is predictable (consistent names and shapes), documented, versioned, secure, hard to misuse, and stable: you can add things without breaking existing callers. Clear error messages, pagination for lists, and sensible limits matter as much as the happy path.
contract, versioning, pagination
A payments API: POST /payments with an amount and currency returns an id and a status. Callers never see how cards are processed.
A menu and a waiter: you order from what is listed, the kitchen's methods stay hidden.

How do you secure an API?
What are the main API styles, and how do I pick one?

REST models resources over HTTP and is the default for public APIs. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need, useful when many different clients need different shapes. gRPC uses compact binary messages over HTTP/2 with strict contracts, good for fast service-to-service calls. Also seen: webhooks (server calls you) and message-based APIs. Choose by who calls it, how much flexibility they need and the performance requirement.
REST, GraphQL, gRPC
Public developer API: REST. Mobile app with varied screens: GraphQL. Internal microservices at high volume: gRPC.
Different ways of ordering: pick from a menu (REST), say exactly which fields you want (GraphQL), or use a fast private phone line between kitchens (gRPC).

What is the difference between REST, GraphQL and gRPC (briefly)?
How do JSON and Protocol Buffers differ as data formats?

JSON is text, human-readable, flexible and universally supported, but larger and slower to parse. Protocol Buffers are a compact binary format described by a schema file, smaller and faster, with built-in rules for adding fields safely. XML and Avro also exist. Choose JSON for public and browser-facing APIs and debugging ease; choose protobuf or Avro for high-volume internal traffic and streams where size and schema evolution matter.
serialization, schema, Avro
The same record: JSON of 300 bytes might become around 100 bytes in protobuf, which matters at billions of messages.
JSON is a note in plain words anyone can read; protobuf is shorthand that both sides must have the key to.
What are the key REST rules a designer should know?

Resources have URLs (/orders/42). Methods carry meaning: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, DELETE removes. GET must not change data. Use status codes properly (200 OK, 201 Created, 400 bad request, 401 not signed in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 429 too many requests, 500 server error). Requests are stateless: each carries what the server needs. Plan for pagination, filtering, versioning and caching headers.
HTTP verbs, status codes, pagination
GET /orders?status=open&limit=20 returns a page of orders and a link to the next page.
Treat things as nouns with addresses, and use a small set of verbs to act on them.

What is a REST API, and what should I know about HTTP methods and status codes?
When is GraphQL a good choice, and what are its risks?

GraphQL gives clients one endpoint where they request exactly the fields and nested data they need, avoiding over- and under-fetching and many round trips. Risks: complex queries can overload the backend (needs depth and cost limits), caching is harder than with REST, and it is easy to create N+1 database calls without batching. Good for varied front ends; less so for simple or heavily cached public APIs.
over-fetching, query cost, batching
A mobile screen needs a user's name, last three orders and each order's status in one request, instead of three REST calls.
One shopping list where you ask for exactly what you need, instead of buying fixed packs.
When is gRPC a good choice, and what are its limits?

gRPC runs over HTTP/2 with protobuf contracts, supporting streaming in both directions, strong typing and generated client code in many languages. It is compact and fast, so it suits internal service-to-service calls. Limits: browsers cannot call it directly without a proxy layer, it is harder to debug by eye, and it needs tooling support at every hop (load balancers must understand HTTP/2).
HTTP/2, protobuf, streaming
An ordering service calls a pricing service 5,000 times a second using gRPC with a shared .proto file.
A private high-speed line between kitchens that both agreed the wording of in advance.
What is idempotency in an API, and how do I implement it?

An operation is idempotent if doing it several times has the same effect as once. Reads, PUT and DELETE are naturally so; POST (create) is not. For payments and orders, clients send a unique idempotency key with each request; the server stores the key and result, and a repeat returns the stored result instead of acting again. It makes timeouts and retries safe.
idempotency key, retries, deduplication
A customer's payment times out and the app retries with the same key. The server sees the key and returns the first charge instead of charging again.
Pressing the lift button twice should not call two lifts.
qa
What is idempotency and why does it matter?
What happens when retries meet a non-idempotent endpoint?

If a client times out and retries a create or payment call that is not protected, the server may do the action twice: two orders, two charges, two emails. Failures to answer are ambiguous, since the first request may have succeeded. The fix combines idempotency keys, unique constraints in the database, and clear status endpoints so clients can check before retrying. Reconciliation jobs catch what slips through.
duplicates, reconciliation, timeouts
A mobile app on a weak connection retries 'place order' three times; the user receives three confirmations and a triple charge.
A guest pressing 'order' again because the screen froze, and two dinners arrive.
How does rate limiting protect an API, and where should it sit?

Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window, protecting servers from abuse, bugs and noisy neighbours and keeping costs predictable. Apply it per user, API key, IP and sometimes per endpoint, at the gateway or edge, with a clear 429 response and a Retry-After header. Common algorithms: token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window and sliding window.
429, token bucket, quota
A free tier gets 60 requests per minute; a client script in a loop receives 429 after the 60th request and must back off.
A bouncer who limits how fast people can enter, so the venue does not get crushed.

What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

Authentication proves identity (password, one-time code, passkey, certificate). Authorization decides what that identity may do (roles, permissions, ownership rules). Many serious flaws are missing authorization checks: the user is signed in, but the code does not check whether this record is theirs. Check both on every request, on the server, not only in the UI.
login, permissions, broken access control
A signed-in customer changes the invoice id in the URL from 123 to 124. If the server only checks 'signed in', they see someone else's invoice.
The front desk checks who you are; your key card decides which rooms you can open.

What do 'authentication' and 'authorization' mean, and why do reviewers care?
What is the difference between session-based and token-based authentication?

In session-based auth, the server stores the login state and gives the browser a session id (cookie); the server looks it up each time. In token-based auth, the server issues a signed token holding the identity and expiry, and any server can verify it without a lookup. Sessions are easy to revoke but need shared storage at scale. Tokens scale easily but are harder to revoke before expiry, so keep them short-lived and use refresh tokens.
cookie, access token, refresh token
A web app uses a secure cookie session. A mobile API uses short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token.
A cloakroom ticket the venue keeps a record of, versus a stamped wristband that proves itself.
What is a JWT, and what are the common mistakes with it?

A JSON Web Token has three parts (header, payload, signature). The signature proves it was issued by a trusted party and not changed, but the payload is only encoded, not secret, so never put sensitive data in it. Mistakes: long expiry times, no way to revoke, storing it where scripts can steal it, accepting unsigned or wrongly algorithmed tokens, and not checking expiry, audience and issuer.
claims, signature, expiry
A token says user 42, role admin, expires in 15 minutes. The API verifies the signature and expiry, then trusts the claims.
A signed passport: anyone can read it, but nobody can alter it without breaking the seal.
What is OAuth 2.0, and what problem does it solve?

OAuth 2.0 lets a user grant an app limited access to their data on another service without sharing their password. The app is redirected to the provider, the user approves specific permissions (scopes), and the app gets an access token (and often a refresh token). In the common authorization-code flow, a short code is exchanged for tokens by the app's server. OAuth is about delegated access; OpenID Connect builds sign-in on top of it.
scopes, authorization code, OIDC
A calendar app asks to 'read your Google Calendar'. You approve; it receives a token limited to that scope.
A valet key: it lets the valet park the car without giving them the master key.

What is OAuth and why does it matter for integrations?
What is single sign-on (SSO), and how does it work?

SSO lets a user sign in once with a central identity provider and then access many applications without signing in again. Apps trust assertions from the provider via standards such as SAML or OpenID Connect. Benefits: fewer passwords, central policies (multi-factor, offboarding), better auditing. Risks: the identity provider becomes critical, so it must be highly available and well protected.
identity provider, SAML, OIDC
An employee logs into Okta or Azure AD in the morning and opens email, wiki and the ticketing tool without more prompts.
One staff badge that opens every door in the building.
What are polling, long polling and server-sent events, and when do I use each?

Polling asks the server repeatedly: simple but wasteful and delayed. Long polling holds each request open until there is data or a timeout, giving near-real-time results over plain HTTP. Server-sent events keep one HTTP connection open for the server to push a stream of messages to the browser, one direction, with automatic reconnect. Use SSE for live feeds and notifications; polling for rare checks.
push, HTTP, reconnect
A live scoreboard uses SSE. A background job status check polls every five seconds.
Asking 'any news?' every minute, asking and waiting at the door until there is news, or having the news delivered through a pipe.
What are WebSockets, and what are their operational challenges?

WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection into a persistent two-way channel, ideal for chat, collaboration, games and live dashboards. Challenges: millions of long-lived connections need memory and sticky routing, load balancers and proxies must support them, deployments drop connections (clients must reconnect and resync), and scaling out needs a shared layer (pub/sub) so a message reaches the right server.
persistent connection, scaling, reconnect
A chat server holds 100,000 connections. A message sent to user B is published to Redis and delivered by whichever server holds B's connection.
A phone call kept open for both sides to talk whenever they like.
What is a webhook, and how do I make one reliable?

A webhook is an HTTP callback: when an event occurs, the provider sends a POST to a URL you registered. To make it reliable, receivers must respond quickly, verify a signature, process idempotently (events can arrive twice or out of order) and queue work. Senders should retry with backoff, log deliveries and offer replay. Never trust the payload without verifying its origin.
callback, signature, retries
A payment provider posts 'payment succeeded'. Your endpoint verifies the signature, stores the event id, returns 200, and processes it from a queue.
The shop phones you when your order is ready, instead of you calling every hour.

What is a webhook and how do you make it reliable?
What is WebRTC, and when is it used?

WebRTC lets browsers and apps exchange audio, video and data directly (peer-to-peer) with low latency. A signalling server helps peers find each other, STUN helps discover public addresses, and TURN relays traffic when a direct path is blocked. Group calls usually use a media server (SFU) so each client uploads once. It uses encryption by default.

Challenges: discovering peers, security and trust, uneven peer quality, NAT traversal and consistency. Used in file sharing (BitTorrent), some video calling, blockchains and parts of content distribution.

What is hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)?

Hexagonal architecture keeps business logic at the centre and talks to the outside world through ports (interfaces) with adapters for each technology (HTTP, database, queue, test fakes). The core does not depend on frameworks or databases, so you can test it easily and swap technologies. It adds some indirection, so it pays off in long-lived systems with significant business logic.

What is CQRS, and when is it worth the complexity?

Command Query Responsibility Segregation separates the model for writes (commands) from the model for reads (queries), so each can be optimised and scaled independently, possibly with different stores. Reads are usually built from events or changes, so they are eventually consistent. It helps when read and write shapes or loads differ a lot; for simple CRUD it is over-engineering.

What is event sourcing, and what are its risks?

Event sourcing stores every change as an immutable event and derives current state by replaying events (with snapshots for speed). Benefits: a full audit trail, the ability to rebuild state and answer 'what did it look like then?'. Risks: event schema evolution, replay time, a steep learning curve, handling corrections, and privacy deletion. Often paired with CQRS.

What is service discovery, and why is it needed?

In dynamic environments, service instances start, stop and change addresses. Service discovery keeps a registry of healthy instances: client-side (the caller looks up and chooses) or server-side (a load balancer or platform does it). Examples: DNS-based discovery, Consul, Kubernetes services. Health checks keep the registry accurate.

What does an API gateway do, and what are its risks?

An API gateway is the front door for clients: routing, authentication, rate limiting, request shaping, TLS, logging and sometimes aggregation of several service calls. It simplifies clients and centralises cross-cutting rules. Risks: it can become a bottleneck or single point of failure, and a place where business logic wrongly accumulates. Run it redundantly and keep it thin.

What is the Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern?

A BFF is a backend layer made for one kind of client (web, mobile, partner), shaping and combining data from services into exactly the responses that client needs. It avoids one generic API serving everyone badly and keeps client logic out of core services. Cost: more services to maintain and the risk of duplicated logic.

What is the sidecar pattern?

A sidecar is a helper process or container deployed next to a service instance that handles cross-cutting functions: logging, metrics, TLS, retries, configuration. The service stays focused, and the same helper works for services in any language. Cost: extra resource use and another component to operate and keep updated. Service meshes are built on sidecars.

Each pod has a proxy sidecar that encrypts traffic and reports metrics, with no change to the app code.
A helper who rides alongside every worker handling the paperwork, so the worker only does the main job.
What is the circuit breaker pattern, and how does it prevent cascading failures?

A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and counts failures. When failures pass a threshold it opens, failing calls immediately (or returning a fallback) instead of waiting and piling up. After a pause it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through; success closes it again. It protects the caller's threads and gives the dependency room to recover.

The recommendation service is slow; after 50% failures the breaker opens, the page shows a default list, and checkout stays fast.

What is the bulkhead pattern?

A bulkhead isolates resources (thread pools, connection pools, queues, even whole clusters) per dependency or per customer, so one slow or failing part cannot use up the shared capacity and starve everything else. It limits blast radius at the cost of some unused capacity. Often combined with timeouts and circuit breakers.

Calls to the reports service get their own pool of 20 threads; if reports hang, checkout calls still have threads.

What is the strangler fig pattern for migrating a legacy system?

Instead of a risky big-bang rewrite, put a routing layer in front of the old system and gradually move features, one slice at a time, to new services. Traffic for migrated routes goes to the new code; the rest still hits the old system, which is retired when empty. It lowers risk and delivers value early, but you run two systems for a while and need data synchronisation.

What is a service mesh, and do I need one?

A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd and similar) uses proxies beside services, managed by a control plane, to provide mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting, observability and policy without changing app code. It is valuable with many services needing consistent security and visibility. It adds complexity, resource cost and a learning curve, so most small systems do not need one.

Why is a distributed system fundamentally harder than a single machine?

Distributed systems face partial failure (some parts fail while others run), unreliable and variable networks, no shared clock, no global view, and unknown whether a silent peer is dead or just slow. Messages can be lost, duplicated, delayed or reordered. Designs must assume these things: timeouts, retries, idempotency, replication, and clear consistency rules.

A client sends a payment request and gets no reply. It cannot know whether the server processed it.
With one cook you know what is happening; with ten cooks in different kitchens you can never be sure what others have done.
What is a network partition, and what is a split-brain problem?

A network partition splits nodes into groups that cannot talk to each other though all are running. Split brain happens when each side believes the other is down and both act as leader, accepting conflicting writes. Avoid it with majority quorums (only the side holding more than half can act), fencing tokens and leases, and a consensus-based leader election.

A 5-node cluster splits 3 and 2. Only the 3-node side has a majority and may elect a leader; the 2-node side stops accepting writes.
The phone line between two offices goes down, and each office thinks it is in charge.

How do heartbeats detect failures, and why is failure detection unreliable?

Nodes send periodic heartbeat messages or are pinged; a node missing several in a row is suspected dead. You cannot tell a crashed node from a slow or partitioned one, so detectors trade speed against false alarms. Tune timeouts, use adaptive detectors (such as phi-accrual), and design so wrongly removing a live node is safe (fencing, idempotent actions).

A garbage-collection pause of 12 seconds makes a healthy node look dead; the cluster elects a new leader while the old one wakes up.

How do distributed systems handle failures in practice?

Core techniques: timeouts on every call; retries with exponential backoff and jitter; idempotent operations; circuit breakers and bulkheads; redundancy and failover; replication; graceful degradation (serve partial results); queues to absorb spikes; and chaos testing to rehearse failures. Always decide what the user sees when a dependency is down.

If recommendations fail, the page still loads with a generic list rather than an error.
Plan for everything that can break: retry, give up politely, use a spare, and never assume.

What are the main consistency models, from strong to eventual?

Linearizability (strong): behaves as if there were one copy, every read sees the latest write. Sequential consistency: all see operations in one order, not necessarily real-time. Causal consistency: effects appear after their causes. Read-your-writes and monotonic reads: per-user guarantees. Eventual consistency: replicas converge if updates stop. Stronger models cost latency and availability; pick the weakest that is still correct.
linearizable, causal, eventual
A user posts a comment and sees it immediately (read-your-writes) even if other users see it a second later.
How up to date everyone's copy of the notice board must be.

Why are physical clocks unreliable for ordering events across machines?

Each machine's clock drifts, and synchronisation protocols (NTP) leave errors from milliseconds up to far more, and clocks can jump backwards. Comparing timestamps from different machines can order events wrongly, so 'last write wins' by wall-clock time can silently lose data. Systems use logical clocks, version vectors or special hardware time with bounded error to order events safely.
clock drift, NTP, last write wins
Machine A's clock is 80 ms ahead of B. A's earlier write carries a later timestamp and wrongly overwrites B's newer write.

What are logical clocks, and what problem do they solve?

A logical clock orders events using counters instead of real time, capturing the happened-before relation: if one event could have influenced another, it is ordered earlier. This gives a consistent ordering without synchronised clocks. Lamport timestamps and vector clocks are the main kinds.
happened-before, ordering
Message A is sent, then B replies. The reply must have a larger logical number than the message it answers.
Numbering events by 'what happened before what', not by the time on a watch.
How do Lamport timestamps work, and what can they not tell you?

Each process keeps a counter, incremented on each local event and sent with messages. On receiving a message, it sets its counter to max(own, received)+1. If event A happened before B then A's timestamp is lower. But a lower timestamp does not prove A happened before B; they might be concurrent. Ties can be broken by process id for a total order.

P1 sends at 5; P2 at 2 receives it and jumps to 6, so its next event is clearly after the send.
Each person keeps a counter and always jumps past any number they hear.
How do vector clocks detect concurrent updates?

Each node keeps a vector of counters, one per node. Local events increment its own entry; messages carry vectors and receivers take the element-wise maximum. Comparing two vectors tells whether one happened before the other or they are concurrent (neither dominates), which means a conflict to resolve. Cost: the vector grows with the number of nodes. Dynamo-style stores used them to expose conflicting versions.
version vector, conflict detection, causality
Two replicas both update a shopping cart; their vectors are incomparable, so the system keeps both versions and merges them.

What is consensus, and why is it hard?

Consensus is getting a group of nodes to agree on a value (such as who the leader is, or the next log entry) despite crashes and message loss. The famous impossibility result (FLP) shows that in a fully asynchronous network no algorithm can guarantee both agreement and termination if even one node may crash; practical algorithms rely on timeouts and quorums. It underpins replicated logs, configuration stores and leader election.

A 5-node cluster agrees that entry 17 of the log is 'set x=3'; once a majority has stored it, it is committed.

How does Paxos work, in plain terms?

Paxos has proposers, acceptors and learners. A proposer sends a numbered 'prepare' request; acceptors promise not to accept lower numbers and report any value they already accepted. The proposer then sends an 'accept' request, with the previously accepted value if there was one, otherwise its own. If a majority accepts, the value is chosen. Safety holds always; progress can stall under competing proposers, which is why practical systems add a stable leader (multi-Paxos).

Two proposers compete; the higher-numbered prepare wins, and a value already accepted by a majority is never replaced.
A committee that first asks 'has anyone already agreed on something?' before proposing its own idea.
How does Raft work, and why is it easier to teach than Paxos?

Raft splits consensus into leader election, log replication and safety. Time is divided into terms; a follower that hears nothing from a leader becomes a candidate and requests votes; a candidate with a majority becomes leader. The leader appends client commands to its log, replicates to followers, and commits an entry once a majority has stored it. Followers with out-of-date logs are repaired by the leader. Used in etcd and Consul.

The leader crashes; after a randomised timeout a follower with an up-to-date log wins the vote for the next term.

How does leader election work, and what are the pitfalls?

Systems elect a leader to coordinate writes or tasks. Methods: consensus (Raft), a coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd) using ephemeral nodes or leases, or bully-style algorithms. Pitfalls: two leaders (split brain), slow detection causing downtime, and the old leader acting after losing leadership. Use leases with expiry, fencing tokens and majority votes.

A job scheduler runs on three nodes; the one that holds the etcd lease schedules jobs, and others stand by.

What are distributed locks, and why are they dangerous?

A distributed lock lets only one process act on a resource at a time across machines, often through Redis, ZooKeeper or etcd with a time-limited lease. Danger: a process may pause (GC, network) beyond its lease, then act while another holds the lock. Mitigate with fencing tokens that the resource checks, short critical sections, and idempotent operations. Prefer designs that avoid locks, such as partitioned ownership or queues.

Two workers both believe they hold the lock after one pauses; a fencing token lets the storage reject the older worker's write.

What is the gossip protocol, and what is it good for?

In gossip protocols each node periodically exchanges state with a few random peers, so information spreads exponentially and reaches all nodes quickly without a central coordinator. It is used for membership, failure detection and spreading metadata in systems such as Cassandra and Consul. It is scalable and resilient, but only eventually consistent and gives probabilistic delivery times.
epidemic, membership, anti-entropy
A node joins and tells two peers; within a few rounds the whole 1,000-node cluster knows about it.
Rumours spreading: each person tells a few random others, and soon everyone knows.
What are CRDTs, and how do they resolve conflicts without coordination?

Conflict-free replicated data types are structures (counters, sets, registers, sequences) whose merge operation is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas can update independently and always converge. Examples: a grow-only counter, an observed-remove set. Trade-offs: metadata overhead, limited semantics, and unusual behaviour in edge cases. Used in collaborative apps, offline-first apps and some databases.
convergence, merge, offline-first
Two phones add items to a shared list while offline; when they reconnect, both sets of additions are merged without losing any.
A shared tally sheet designed so everyone's edits can be combined in any order and give the same total.
What is operational transformation, and how does it compare with CRDTs?

Operational transformation (OT) lets concurrent edits to a document be transformed against each other so all copies converge, classically through a central server that orders operations; it powered early collaborative editors. CRDTs achieve convergence by data-structure design without needing a central order. OT is mature but its transform functions are hard to get right; CRDTs trade larger metadata for simplicity and offline support.
collaborative editing, convergence
Two users insert text at the same position; transforms shift one insert so both appear and the final text matches everywhere.
Editors adjusting each other's edits so that everyone ends with the same document.

Why are transactions across services or databases so hard?

A single database gives ACID transactions. Once data lives in several services or databases, there is no shared transaction: a step can succeed in one place and fail in another, leaving the system half-updated. The coordinator or participant can crash mid-way, messages can be lost, and locks held across the network hurt performance. You must choose between coordinated protocols (2PC), compensating workflows (saga), or redesigning so one transaction suffices.

Order service saves the order, then the payment service call times out. Is the customer charged or not?
Two shops must both agree to a swap, but a phone line can drop between them.

How does two-phase commit (2PC) work, and what are its drawbacks?

In phase one, the coordinator asks participants to prepare (they durably record they can commit and hold locks). In phase two, if all agreed, the coordinator tells them to commit; otherwise to abort. It gives atomic commit across participants. Drawbacks: it blocks if the coordinator crashes after prepare, holds locks (hurting throughput), adds latency, and couples services. It is used inside databases and some XA setups, but rarely across public microservices.

A transfer touches two databases: both prepare, the coordinator commits both. If it crashes between, participants wait holding locks.
The organiser asks everyone 'can you do it?' and only when all say yes says 'do it now'.
What is three-phase commit, and why is it rarely used?

3PC adds a pre-commit phase between prepare and commit so participants can decide safely after a coordinator failure, reducing blocking. It assumes bounded delays and does not remain correct under network partitions, and it costs more messages. In practice, consensus-based commit or sagas are used instead.
non-blocking, pre-commit, partitions
The coordinator crashes after pre-commit; participants can proceed to commit rather than wait, if the network is well-behaved.
Adding an extra 'about to commit' step so people are less stuck if the organiser disappears.
What is the saga pattern, and how does it handle failure?

A saga splits a business transaction into local transactions in each service. If a step fails, previously completed steps are undone with compensating actions (refund, release stock). Two styles: choreography (services react to each other's events) and orchestration (a coordinator drives the steps). Sagas give eventual consistency, not isolation, so intermediate states are visible and compensations must be idempotent.
compensation, orchestration, choreography
Place order, reserve stock, charge card. Charge fails, so release the stock and cancel the order.
A multi-step holiday booking where, if the hotel fails, you cancel the flight you already booked.
What is the transactional outbox pattern, and what problem does it fix?

A service must update its database and publish an event, but doing both separately can fail halfway (data saved, event lost, or the reverse). The outbox pattern writes the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the data change. A separate relay (a poller or change data capture) reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, at least once. Consumers must therefore be idempotent.

Order saved and 'OrderPlaced' written to the outbox in one transaction; a relay publishes it, retrying until acknowledged.
Writing the letter in the same notebook as the ledger entry, so a clerk later posts every letter that was written.
What happens when a saga's compensation also fails?

Compensation can fail like any step. Retry it with backoff (it must be idempotent), keep the saga state durable so it can resume after a crash, route persistent failures to a dead letter queue or a manual-review queue, and alert people. Design compensations so they cannot be impossible (a sent email cannot be unsent, so confirm it last). Reconciliation jobs detect and fix leftover mismatches.

The refund call fails because the payment provider is down. The saga retries for hours, then flags the order for finance review.

What is a geohash, and what is it used for?

A geohash encodes a latitude and longitude into a short string by repeatedly halving the map. Places that share a prefix are in the same rectangle, so you can find nearby points with a prefix lookup in a normal index. Weaknesses: points close together across a cell edge have very different codes (so you check neighbouring cells too), cells are rectangles that distort near the poles, and sizes are fixed steps.

Two cafes with geohashes 'tdr1w' and 'tdr1y' share a prefix, so a prefix search finds both for 'near me'.
A postcode for the whole planet: longer codes mean smaller areas, and nearby places share the same beginning.

What is a quadtree, and when does it beat a fixed grid?

A quadtree divides a 2D space into four quadrants and subdivides any quadrant holding too many points. It adapts to uneven density, so crowded areas get fine cells and empty areas stay coarse. Range and nearest-neighbour searches walk only the relevant cells. Updates need rebalancing, and it is usually held in memory. Good for maps, games and location services with uneven distributions.

A food-delivery app finds all drivers within 2 km by walking only the few small cells around the customer.
A map that zooms in only where it is crowded: a busy city is cut into many small squares, empty desert stays one big square.
What are R-trees, and how do they differ from quadtrees?

An R-tree groups nearby objects into minimum bounding rectangles, nested hierarchically and balanced like a B-tree, so it works well on disk and handles rectangles and areas, not just points. Queries skip any box that does not overlap the search area. Used in spatial databases (PostGIS uses R-tree-style indexes). Overlapping boxes can slow queries.

What are S2 and H3, and why do big map systems use them?

S2 (from Google) maps the sphere onto a cube and uses a space-filling curve to give each cell a 64-bit id, supporting hierarchical cells and region covering. H3 (from Uber) tiles the globe with hexagons at many resolutions; hexagons have uniform neighbour distances, which suits analytics and surge pricing. Both turn 2D proximity into simple id lookups, avoiding the edge problems of geohashes.

What is a Bloom filter, and what does a 'maybe' mean?

A Bloom filter is a compact bit array and several hash functions that tests set membership. If any checked bit is 0 the item is definitely absent; if all are 1 it is probably present, with a tunable false-positive rate (roughly 10 bits per item gives about 1%). It never gives false negatives and cannot remove items (counting variants can). Used to skip disk lookups for missing keys, in caches, LSM databases and crawlers.

What is a cuckoo filter, and how does it compare with a Bloom filter?

A cuckoo filter stores short fingerprints of items in a cuckoo-hash table. Like a Bloom filter it answers 'probably present or definitely absent', but it supports deletion and can use less space at low false-positive rates. Inserts may relocate fingerprints, and a full table can fail an insert. Choose it when you need deletes or tight space.

What is a skip list, and where is it used?

A skip list is a sorted linked list with extra layers of 'express' pointers chosen randomly, so searches, inserts and deletes take about O(log n) on average without complex rebalancing. It is simple to make concurrent. Used in in-memory sorted structures such as Redis sorted sets and memtables of LSM stores.

What is a count-min sketch, and what can it count?

A count-min sketch is a table of counters addressed by several hash functions. To count an item you increment one counter per row; to estimate, you take the minimum across rows. It may overestimate (collisions) but never underestimates, and uses fixed small memory. Used for frequency estimates and heavy hitters (top-k) in streams, network monitoring and trending topics.

Counting the most-searched queries over a day of billions of searches without storing each distinct query.
A small set of tally boards where a popular item is marked on every board, so the smallest tally is a good estimate.
What is HyperLogLog, and how does it count unique items so cheaply?

HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements (cardinality) by hashing each item and tracking, in many small registers, the maximum count of leading zero bits seen. Rare long runs suggest many distinct items. It uses a few kilobytes for billions of items, with a small relative error (around 1 to 2%), and sketches can be merged. What are Merkle trees, and how do they help sync and verify data?

A Merkle tree hashes each data block, then hashes pairs of hashes up to a single root. Two replicas compare roots; if they match, all data matches. If not, they compare child hashes to locate the differing blocks with few comparisons. Used for anti-entropy repair (Dynamo-style stores), Git, blockchains and verifying downloads, since a proof needs only a path of hashes.

Two replicas of a million rows compare roots, then drill down to find the 3 rows that differ.
A tree of fingerprints: compare the top fingerprint, and if it differs, drill down to find the exact page that changed.
What is MinHash, and what is it used for?

MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity (overlap divided by union) between sets by keeping the minimum hash value under many hash functions. The fraction of matching minima approximates similarity. With locality-sensitive hashing, it finds near-duplicate documents quickly. Used in duplicate detection, plagiarism checks and recommendation candidates. What is the difference between batch and stream processing?

Batch processing handles large chunks of data on a schedule: high throughput, simple, results delayed (minutes to hours). Stream processing handles events continuously with low delay, needing state, windowing, ordering and late-data handling. Use batch for reports and training; streaming for alerts, fraud checks and live dashboards. Many systems combine both.

What is change data capture (CDC), and why is it useful?

CDC captures inserts, updates and deletes from a database (usually by reading its transaction log) and streams them to other systems: caches, search indexes, warehouses and event streams. It avoids heavy batch queries and dual writes and keeps copies in sync with low delay. Considerations: schema changes, ordering, initial snapshots, and delivery at least once.

What is MapReduce, and why does it still matter conceptually?

MapReduce processes large data in parallel: the map step turns records into key-value pairs on many machines, the framework shuffles them so equal keys meet, and the reduce step aggregates per key. It brought fault-tolerant processing across commodity clusters. Spark and others replaced the disk-heavy original, but the map, shuffle and reduce thinking still underlies distributed group-by and joins.

What is an ETL pipeline, and how does it differ from ELT?

ETL extracts data from sources, transforms it (clean, join, aggregate) on a separate engine, and loads it into the target. ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse, taking advantage of its power and keeping raw history. Key concerns: idempotent reruns, schema changes, data quality checks, lineage and orchestration.

What are data lakes, data warehouses and lakehouses?

A data lake stores raw, varied data cheaply (usually object storage) and applies structure when read. A data warehouse stores curated, structured data optimised for analytics and SQL. A lakehouse adds warehouse-like features (tables, transactions, schema enforcement) on top of lake storage via formats such as Delta, Iceberg or Hudi. What are the Lambda and Kappa architectures?

Lambda runs a batch layer (accurate, slow) and a speed layer (fast, approximate) and merges results, at the cost of two code paths. Kappa treats everything as a stream: one pipeline, with reprocessing done by replaying the log. Kappa is simpler but needs a replayable log and a capable streaming engine. Modern streaming engines have made Kappa-style designs more common.

What do streaming engines like Kafka Streams, Flink and Spark Structured Streaming do?

Streaming engines process unbounded event streams with stateful operations: windows (tumbling, sliding, session), joins, aggregations, event-time handling with watermarks for late data, checkpoints for recovery, and delivery guarantees. Flink is built for low-latency stateful streaming; Spark Structured Streaming uses micro-batches and shares APIs with batch; Kafka Streams is a library running inside your application. Correctness depends on event time, state size and checkpointing.

How do rolling deployments work, and what can go wrong?

A rolling deployment updates instances in batches while the others serve traffic, with health checks between batches. It needs no extra environment, but old and new versions run side by side, so they must be compatible (APIs and database). Rollback is slower, and a bad version may serve some users before detection. How does a blue-green deployment work, and what does it cost?

You keep two production environments. Blue serves traffic; green gets the new version and is tested; then traffic switches, usually at the router or load balancer, with an instant switch back if problems appear. Costs: double the infrastructure during the switch and careful handling of the shared database, in-flight requests and sessions.

A canary release sends a small share of real traffic (1 to 5%) to the new version, compares it with the old on health signals (errors, latency, business metrics), and expands in steps or rolls back automatically. It limits the blast radius and tests with real traffic. Needs good monitoring, enough traffic for the signal to be meaningful, and sticky user assignment to avoid confusing users.

How does distributed tracing work?

A trace id is created at the entry point and propagated in headers through every service call and queue message. Each service records spans (operation, start, duration, status) tied to that id. A tracing backend assembles the spans into a timeline, showing where time went and where errors began. Challenges: propagating context everywhere (including async work), sampling to control cost, and consistent instrumentation.
